frameworks.name: Work = Volume × Leverage
frameworks.definition: Output is the product of repetition volume and per-instance return; volume drives skill acquisition, which then increases leverage per instance, creating a compounding cycle.

frameworks.name: Requisites-for-Focus Framework
frameworks.definition: Only activities that sustain direct focus on the primary goal (sleep, food, basic needs) are productive; all other activities are distractions. Rest becomes requisite and therefore productive when it enables continued output on the core mission.

claims.text: Work equals volume multiplied by leverage. Early growth requires executing at 10-100x the volume of competitors while building skill; the same volume repeated over time yields exponentially higher leverage per unit of effort (Hormozi, observed in personal brand scaling and billionaire founder coaching).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Early-stage business or personal brand growth
Domain not yet saturated by competitor volume
claims.mechanism: High-volume repetition forces skill acquisition; skill consolidation compounds leverage-per-unit, enabling same-volume output to yield disproportionate returns.

anchors.value: 10x initial volume (example: 450 pieces per week vs. competitor baseline)
7 pieces per week, competing against Hormozi producing 450

bounded_by: Domain-specific: the 100x insight learned in one domain does not auto-transfer; it must be re-learned per new context

claims.text: Working longer hours produces superior daily output quality and quantity compared to younger years because the skill of working itself improves with repetition. People who report low productivity when working are usually not working enough; the work-skill muscle requires practice through extended, uncomfortable sessions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Extended work periods (100+ consecutive days or similar intensity)
Sustained effort beyond initial fatigue threshold
claims.mechanism: Repetition of the work activity builds the meta-skill of working (focus, output quality, endurance). The ability to return to focus after a temporary drop in energy is a learnable skill that requires practice under discomfort.

numbers.axis: days worked consecutively in a period

anchors.value: 100 consecutive days with zero days off
3-4 days off total since Jan 1, with work until 2 AM on some of those days

claims.text: Focus fatigue (the craving to stop work, break concentration, or rest) typically lasts 5-20 minutes; learning to push through this threshold 10-15 times per work session is trainable and does not require willpower, only practice. The same neurochemical craving pattern occurs during dieting and is equally manageable through repetition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Operator has basic biological needs met (sleep, food)

numbers.axis: duration of focus craving or urge to stop (minutes)

bounded_by: Does not apply to sleep deprivation or malnutrition contexts where biological need is unmet

claims.text: The ability to continue working after a temporary mental/focus checkout—to 'whip your head back in'—is a trainable muscle developed only through practicing it under the exact condition where it is needed: sustained discomfort, fatigue, or distraction. Three to six additional hours of output often follow the breakthrough through one such threshold.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Extended work session (multi-hour, continuous focus required)
Operator has basic biological needs met
claims.mechanism: Practicing the redirect-to-focus maneuver under exactly the condition it will be needed (fatigue, mental checkout) strengthens the neural pathway for that redirect. Without practice under discomfort, the skill does not transfer to real scenarios.

claims.text: Historical precedent demonstrates humans are physiologically capable of working continuously for years on end. Ancestral humans worked during all waking hours; modern discomfort around continuous work is psychological, not biological. The premise 'you will work until you die because everyone dies and most will work at some point' reframes continuous effort as a logical state rather than an exception.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Biological needs (food, sleep, shelter) are met
bounded_by: Does not apply to coerced or survival-threat-based work (e.g., work-or-die contexts)
Assumes access to modern comfort; ancestral comparison is illustrative but not prescriptive for modern conditions

claims.text: The idea 'do what you love and you'll never work another day in your life' is false. Most work is neither pleasant nor unpleasant; it is simply work. Motivation should derive from the tangible past achievements that prove the current uncomfortable work will pay off, not from emotional resonance with the task itself.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Work includes non-preferred but necessary tasks
bounded_by: Does not apply to work that is actively harmful or poses health risk

claims.text: Sleep deprivation is variable: working on 5-6 hours of sleep is sustainable and acceptable; 9 hours of sleep after extended work is restorative but rare. The quality and focus of work produced on 5-6 hours is materially lower than on 7-8 hours, but the gap is quantifiable and the work remains productive.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sleep deprivation is temporary (days to weeks, not months)
Biological need for food is met

claims.text: Rest and eating, while necessary for survival and focus, are requisites for forward progress on the primary goal—not distractions from it. Only activities that do not sustain the capacity for deep work on the core mission are distractions. This reframes rest as productive investment, not as lost work time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Operator has a clearly defined core mission
Rest and eating measurably restore capacity for that mission
bounded_by: Does not apply to rest that exceeds basic recovery needs or enables avoidance behaviors

claims.text: Skill and output quality compound with extended work. A legal intern at Arkema (France) was told by a senior partner 'you don't even know what work is' despite spending the whole summer working intensively. The partner's point was that the intern was spending time but producing little; only repetition and accumulated reps teach the skill of working itself, distinct from the work content.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Extended time investment (full season or longer) has been made

examples.text: Hormozi was told by a large brand strategist that his personal brand growth was slow. When the strategist pulled up both Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube profiles side by side, the diagnosis was immediate: the strategist had been producing 10 times more volume than Hormozi. Hormozi acknowledged the gap and applied the 100x principle instead of 2x, eventually reaching a state where he produced 450 pieces per week. Later, when advising a billionaire founder entering the content space, Hormozi showed the same comparison—himself at 450 pieces per week versus the billionaire at 7 pieces per week—and the billionaire, having learned the 100x lesson in a different domain (business), immediately understood the gap.

Hormozi worked 100 consecutive days without a day off at the start of 2026, followed by approximately 3-4 days off for the entire year while still working until 2 AM on some of those off-days. The distinction between working all the time when younger and working all the time now is that the daily output and quality are significantly higher—the skill of working itself has compounded. When the mind checks out mid-task, Hormozi continues anyway, and often 3-6 hours of additional work emerge before the task is finished.

When dieting, a craving for food or sweets typically lasts less than 20 minutes. The parallel to focus fatigue is direct: when you feel the urge to stop working and take a break or watch Netflix, that urge usually lasts only 5-20 minutes. Most people yield to the urge, but the urge itself is temporary and trainable. Hormozi sets a timer when a dieting craving strikes; the same mechanism applies to focus.

practices.text: When working and you feel the urge to stop, set a timer for 20 minutes. Most cravings for rest or distraction pass within that window without action. If the urge persists after 20 minutes, reassess; otherwise, continue.
Every activity that does not sustain capacity for your core mission is a distraction. Actively audit your daily and weekly schedule to identify and eliminate non-requisite activities.

When learning a new skill or domain, apply the 100x principle (not 2x): produce 10-100 times the volume your competitors are producing in the early phase. This is domain-specific and must be re-learned per new context.

Use past achievements and completed projects as fuel for motivation in the present moment, especially when the work is uncomfortable or unpleasant. The tangible proof that effort pays off is more reliable than emotional resonance with the task.
